newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan refugees displaced by Badghis fighting.
newsitem.headline: Afghan refugees displaced by Badghis fighting.

text.p: The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) says that 100 refugee families per day are fleeing fighting and arriving in the town of Herat in northwestern Afghanistan.
Forces of the puritanical Islamic Taleban are facing fighters loyal to the alliance of General Abdul Rashid Dostum and the ousted government in the remote nothwestern provinces of Badghis and Faryab.
"A hundred families are arriving each day in Herat." Jean-Luc Paladini, press officer for the ICRC in Kabul, said on Saturday. "They have been displaced by the fighting in Badghis." said Paladini.
Paladini estimated that some 1,500 families - approximately 10,500 people - had arrived in Taleban-held Herat since fighting broke out at the beginning of November.
"Our latest estimate is that there are 1,100 families in three United Nations camps just outside Herat and another 400 families staying inside the city itself." Paladini told Reuters.
International oganisations in Afghanistan estimate that the average family has seven members.
The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) is organising an emergency airlift of relief supplies to Herat to help the situation.
The UNHCR estimates that about 50,000 people have been displaced by the fighting.
Paladini said the ICRC, in collaboration with the Afghan Red Crescent Society, would start distributing food, blankets and plastic sheeting to the refugee families in Herat itself.

"A first convoy, carrying 200 tonnes of food, is on its way to Herat," said Paladini. "This is the first time we have had to distribute food in Herat. A second convoy carrying 3,000 blankets, plastic sheeting, candles and matches will leave soon."
Paladini said the UN would concentrate on refugees in the camps while the Red Cross provided aid for families in the city.
He said Red Cross and Red Crescent workers would visit each of the families to assess their needs and that they hoped to have the first distribution on November 30.
There has been claim and counter-claims of victory by both sides in the battle in the northwest, but it has been impossible to verify either side's comments.
Taleban-controlled radio in Kabul said on Friday night that their forces had shot down a plane belonging to Dostum in Badghis and captured the pilot.
Radio Shariat said that they had used an American-made Stinger missile to shoot down the plane, but it was not possible to check the report.

The United States provided some 1,000 Stinger heat-seeking ground-to-air missiles to the Afghan mujahideen during their fight against the communists. Afghan watchers believe that many of the missiles are still in Afghanistan.
